title: Linear algebra complete reference: vector spaces, rank, determinants, factorisations
tagline: Every linear-algebra object the ML syllabus names, with the one fact you must remember about each.
explain:
**Scalars, vectors, matrices, tensors.** A scalar is a number, a vector $x\in\mathbb R^n$ a column of numbers, a matrix $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ a grid, a tensor an $n$-dimensional array (images are $H\times W\times C$). Matrix multiplication $C=AB$ with $C_{ij}=\sum_kA_{ik}B_{kj}$ requires inner dimensions to match, is associative and distributive but **not commutative**. Transpose: $(AB)^\top=B^\top A^\top$. Inverse: $AA^{-1}=I$, exists only for square full-rank matrices, $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$.

**Linear independence, span, basis, dimension.** Vectors $v_1..v_k$ are independent if $\sum c_iv_i=0$ only for $c=0$. A **basis** is an independent set that spans the space; the number of vectors is the **dimension**. Every vector has unique coordinates in a basis. Changing basis is multiplying by an invertible matrix; PCA picks the basis aligned with variance.

**Rank.** $\mathrm{rank}(A)$ = number of independent columns = independent rows = number of non-zero singular values. Rank-nullity: $\mathrm{rank}(A)+\dim\mathrm{null}(A)=n$. Full-rank square matrix ⇔ invertible ⇔ $\det A\ne0$. Low rank means redundancy - the reason compression (SVD, LoRA) works.

**Determinant.** $\det A$ is the signed volume-scaling factor of the map; $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$, $\det A^{-1}=1/\det A$, $\det A=\prod\lambda_i$. Zero determinant ⇒ space collapsed, singular. In ML it appears in Gaussian densities ($|\Sigma|^{-1/2}$) and flows ($\log|\det J|$).

**Norms and distances.** $\|x\|_p=(\sum|x_i|^p)^{1/p}$: $\ell_1$ (Manhattan, sparsity), $\ell_2$ (Euclidean), $\ell_\infty$ (max). Matrix norms: Frobenius $\sqrt{\sum a_{ij}^2}$, spectral $\sigma_{\max}$. Distances: Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine, Mahalanobis $\sqrt{(x-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)}$ (accounts for correlation).

**Projections and orthogonality.** Projection of $b$ onto the column space of $A$: $p=A(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top b$ - the least-squares solution. Vectors are orthogonal if $x^\top y=0$. An **orthogonal matrix** satisfies $Q^\top Q=I$ (rotations/reflections, preserves lengths, $Q^{-1}=Q^\top$). Gram-Schmidt builds an orthonormal basis (QR decomposition).

**Eigen and definiteness.** $Av=\lambda v$. A symmetric matrix is **positive definite (PD)** if $x^\top Ax>0\ \forall x\ne0$ ⇔ all $\lambda>0$ ⇔ Cholesky $A=LL^\top$ exists; **PSD** if $\ge0$. Covariance matrices and kernel (Gram) matrices are PSD; a PD Hessian means a strict local minimum. **Spectral theorem**: symmetric $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$.

**Matrix factorisations**: **LU** ($A=LU$, solving linear systems), **QR** (stable least squares), **Cholesky** (PD systems, sampling Gaussians, $O(n^3/3)$), **eigendecomposition**, **SVD** ($A=U\Sigma V^\top$, any matrix; pseudo-inverse $A^+=V\Sigma^{+}U^\top$), **NMF** ($V\approx WH$, non-negative parts-based features), **matrix factorisation for recommenders** ($R\approx UV^\top$, minimise $\|R-UV^\top\|^2_\Omega+\lambda(\|U\|^2+\|V\|^2)$ by ALS/SGD).

**Solving $Ax=b$**: unique if $A$ invertible; least squares if overdetermined ($m>n$): $x=(A^\top A)^{-1}A^\top b$ or via QR/SVD; minimum-norm if underdetermined ($x=A^+b$). Condition number $\kappa=\sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}$ measures sensitivity to perturbations.
tradeoffs: Direct methods (LU/QR/Cholesky) are exact but $O(n^3)$; iterative methods (conjugate gradient) scale to huge sparse systems.
Normal equations are cheap but square the condition number; QR/SVD are more stable but slower.
pitfalls: Inverting a matrix to solve a system (use a solver).
Treating a near-singular matrix as invertible - check the condition number.
Mixing row/column-vector conventions between papers and code.
interview: Why is a covariance matrix positive semi-definite?
What does the rank of a weight matrix tell you about the layer?
use: Reading any ML derivation; checking whether a solve/inversion is safe; understanding why PCA, LoRA and kernels work.
avoid: Do not compute explicit inverses in code; do not trust a determinant near zero as a singularity test (use rank/condition).

qa.q: Why is $\det(A)=0$ equivalent to not invertible?
qa.a: $\det A$ is the volume scale of the map. If it is 0 the map flattens some direction to zero (nontrivial null space), so two different inputs map to the same output and no inverse can exist.

qa.q: Show a covariance matrix is PSD.
qa.a: For any $a$: $a^\top\Sigma a=\mathrm{Var}(a^\top X)\ge0$ because it is the variance of a scalar random variable.

title: Calculus complete reference: limits, derivatives, Taylor series, integration, vector calculus
tagline: From limits to Hessians: the calculus that optimisation, probability and backprop rest on.
explain:
**Functions, limits, continuity.** $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ means $f$ gets arbitrarily close to $L$. $f$ is continuous at $a$ if the limit equals $f(a)$. Neural nets with ReLU are continuous but not differentiable at 0 (subgradients are used).

**Derivatives.** $f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}h$. Rules: sum, product $(fg)'=f'g+fg'$, quotient, **chain rule** $(f\circ g)'=f'(g)g'$. Useful: $(e^x)'=e^x$, $(\ln x)'=1/x$, $\sigma'=\sigma(1-\sigma)$, $\tanh'=1-\tanh^2$.

**Multivariable.** Partial derivative $\partial f/\partial x_i$; **gradient** $\nabla f$ (direction of steepest ascent, orthogonal to level sets); **directional derivative** $D_uf=\nabla f\cdot u$ for unit $u$ (maximal when $u\parallel\nabla f$); **Jacobian** $J_{ij}=\partial f_i/\partial x_j$ for vector functions; **Hessian** $H_{ij}=\partial^2f/\partial x_i\partial x_j$ (symmetric; curvature).

**Maxima and minima.** Critical point: $\nabla f=0$. Second-derivative test: $H\succ0$ ⇒ local min; $H\prec0$ ⇒ local max; indefinite ⇒ **saddle**. A function is **convex** if $H\succeq0$ everywhere; then every local minimum is global. In deep nets saddles are far more common than bad local minima. Local vs global optimisation: gradient methods find local solutions; convexity, restarts or global methods (metaheuristics, Bayesian optimisation) are needed for global guarantees.

**Taylor series.** $f(x+\delta)\approx f(x)+\nabla f^\top\delta+\tfrac12\delta^\top H\delta+\dots$ Gradient descent uses the first-order term; Newton's method minimises the second-order model: $\delta=-H^{-1}\nabla f$. The Taylor view also gives the learning-rate bound $\eta<2/\lambda_{\max}(H)$ and linearisation ideas behind LIME and NTK.

**Integration.** $\int_a^bf(x)dx$ is area under the curve; fundamental theorem links it to derivatives. In ML: probabilities are integrals of densities ($P(a<X<b)=\int_a^bp(x)dx$), expectations $\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int g\,p$, marginals $p(x)=\int p(x,z)dz$, evidence $p(D)=\int p(D|\theta)p(\theta)d\theta$ - usually intractable, hence Monte Carlo, variational inference. Techniques: substitution, integration by parts, change of variables (Jacobian determinant), Gaussian integral $\int e^{-x^2/2}dx=\sqrt{2\pi}$. **Monte Carlo**: $\mathbb E[g(X)]\approx\frac1N\sum g(x_i)$ with error $\propto1/\sqrt N$.

**Vector calculus.** Divergence $\nabla\cdot F$, curl $\nabla\times F$, Laplacian $\nabla^2f=\sum\partial^2f/\partial x_i^2$ (appears in PDEs, graph Laplacians, PINNs, Gaussian smoothing). Gradient of a quadratic $\tfrac12x^\top Ax-b^\top x$ is $Ax-b$ (A symmetric) - solved by $x=A^{-1}b$.

**Automatic differentiation vs numerical vs symbolic**: autodiff applies the chain rule exactly on the computation graph (reverse mode for many parameters, forward mode for few); numerical differences are approximate; symbolic can explode in size.
tradeoffs: Second-order methods converge in fewer steps but need Hessians ($O(n^2)$ memory) - impractical for deep nets without approximations.
Monte Carlo is dimension-free but slow ($1/\sqrt N$).
pitfalls: Confusing a critical point with a minimum (check the Hessian).
Forgetting the Jacobian determinant in a change of variables.
Using finite differences with the wrong step size.
interview: Why does gradient descent follow the negative gradient?
What does the Hessian's eigenvalue spectrum say about the loss landscape?
Derive Newton's update from the Taylor expansion.
use: Deriving losses and gradients; reasoning about curvature, convexity and step sizes; reading probabilistic derivations.
avoid: Do not assume a loss is convex because it is smooth.

title: Probability complete reference: distributions, CDF, covariance, correlation, LLN, CLT, MLE
tagline: All the probability named in the syllabus, organised as one toolbox with formulas and when to use each distribution.
explain:
**Basics.** Sample space, events, axioms (non-negativity, $P(\Omega)=1$, additivity). $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. **Conditional**: $P(A|B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$; **chain rule** $P(A,B,C)=P(A)P(B|A)P(C|A,B)$; **total probability** $P(B)=\sum_iP(B|A_i)P(A_i)$; **Bayes** $P(A|B)=P(B|A)P(A)/P(B)$. Independence $P(A,B)=P(A)P(B)$; conditional independence is the backbone of graphical models and Naive Bayes.

**Random variables, PMF/PDF/CDF.** Discrete: PMF $p(x)=P(X=x)$. Continuous: density $f(x)\ge0$, $\int f=1$, $P(a<X<b)=\int_a^bf$. **CDF** $F(x)=P(X\le x)$, monotone, $f=F'$; the **quantile function** $F^{-1}$ gives percentiles and enables inverse-transform sampling.

**Moments.** $\mathbb E[X]$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2$, skewness, kurtosis. Linearity: $\mathbb E[aX+bY]=a\mathbb EX+b\mathbb EY$; $\mathrm{Var}(aX)=a^2\mathrm{Var}X$. **Covariance** $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[(X-\mu_X)(Y-\mu_Y)]$; **correlation** $\rho=\mathrm{Cov}/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)\in[-1,1]$ measures *linear* association only (zero correlation does not imply independence; independence implies zero correlation). $\mathrm{Var}(X+Y)=\mathrm{Var}X+\mathrm{Var}Y+2\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$.

**Joint, marginal, conditional distributions.** $p(x)=\sum_yp(x,y)$ (or $\int$); $p(y|x)=p(x,y)/p(x)$. Multivariate Gaussian $\mathcal N(\mu,\Sigma)$: marginals and conditionals are Gaussian; conditional $\mu_{a|b}=\mu_a+\Sigma_{ab}\Sigma_{bb}^{-1}(x_b-\mu_b)$ (basis of Gaussian processes and Kalman filters).

**Key distributions** (know pmf, mean, variance, use): **Bernoulli**($p$): coin; **Binomial**($n,p$): $np$, $np(1-p)$; **Poisson**($\lambda$): counts/rare events, mean=var=$\lambda$; **Geometric**; **Uniform**; **Exponential**($\lambda$): waiting times, memoryless; **Gaussian**; **Beta**($\alpha,\beta$): a distribution over probabilities (conjugate prior of Bernoulli); **Gamma**; **Dirichlet** (prior over categorical); **Categorical/Multinomial**; **Student-t** (heavy tails, small samples); **Chi-square**; **Laplace**; **Log-normal** (multiplicative effects, latencies).

**Law of large numbers**: $\bar X_n\to\mu$. **Central limit theorem**: $\sqrt n(\bar X_n-\mu)/\sigma\to\mathcal N(0,1)$ for i.i.d. finite-variance data - the justification for confidence intervals and z/t-tests. Concentration: Markov, Chebyshev, Hoeffding.

**Estimation.** **MLE**: $\hat\theta=\arg\max\sum\log p(x_i|\theta)$ (Gaussian: sample mean and (biased) variance; Bernoulli: $k/n$). Properties: consistent, asymptotically normal, efficient. **MAP** adds a prior; **Bayesian** keeps the full posterior. **Method of moments** matches sample and theoretical moments. Bias of an estimator $=\mathbb E\hat\theta-\theta$; unbiased variance uses $n-1$.

**Sampling**: inverse CDF, rejection sampling, importance sampling, MCMC (Metropolis-Hastings, Gibbs).
tradeoffs: Parametric distributions are compact but wrong if misspecified; non-parametric (KDE, empirical) are flexible but data-hungry.
Conjugate priors give closed-form posteriors at the cost of modelling freedom.
pitfalls: Reading correlation as causation or as full dependence.
Using a Gaussian for heavy-tailed data (income, latency).
Mixing up PDF values (can exceed 1) with probabilities.
Treating samples as independent when they are autocorrelated.
interview: Zero correlation vs independence - give a counterexample.
Why does the CLT justify a confidence interval?
When would you choose Poisson vs Binomial?
use: Choosing noise models and priors; understanding every likelihood-based loss; analysing results statistically.
avoid: Do not call data 'normal' without a Q-Q plot or test; do not compute correlations on non-monotone relations without plotting.

qa.a: $X\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$, $Y=X^2$: $\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[X^3]-0=0$, yet $Y$ is a deterministic function of $X$.

title: Statistics complete reference: descriptive, inferential, hypothesis tests, correlation, Bayesian statistics, bootstrap, power
tagline: From describing data to testing claims - the statistics every empirical paper uses.
explain:
**Descriptive statistics.** Location: mean, median, mode, trimmed mean. Spread: variance, standard deviation, IQR, range, MAD. Shape: skewness, kurtosis. Visualisation: histogram, box plot, violin, Q-Q plot, scatter matrix. Prefer the median/IQR for skewed or outlier-ridden data.

**Populations, samples, sampling.** Statistics describe the sample; **inference** generalises to the population. Sampling designs: simple random, stratified (preserve class proportions), cluster, systematic, convenience (biased). The **standard error** of the mean is $s/\sqrt n$.

**Confidence intervals.** For a mean: $\bar x\pm t_{n-1,1-\alpha/2}\,s/\sqrt n$. Meaning: 95% of intervals built this way cover the true value (it is *not* a 95% probability for this single interval).

**Hypothesis testing framework.** State $H_0$ (no effect) and $H_1$; choose significance level $\alpha$ (usually 0.05); compute a test statistic; the **p-value** is $P(\text{data at least this extreme}\mid H_0)$. Reject $H_0$ if $p<\alpha$. **Type I** error = false positive (rate $\alpha$), **Type II** = false negative (rate $\beta$), **power** $=1-\beta$. Statistical significance ≠ practical significance: report **effect size** and CI.

**Common tests**: **z-test** (known $\sigma$ or large $n$); **one-sample t**; **two-sample (Welch) t** $t=\frac{\bar x_1-\bar x_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}$; **paired t** (same units measured twice - differences); **chi-square** test of independence for categorical tables $\chi^2=\sum\frac{(O-E)^2}{E}$ and goodness-of-fit; **ANOVA** compares 3+ group means via $F=\frac{\text{between-group variance}}{\text{within-group variance}}$ (then post-hoc Tukey); **F-test** for variances.

**Correlation.** **Pearson** $r$ (linear, assumes roughly normal, sensitive to outliers); **Spearman** $\rho$ (rank-based, monotonic); **Kendall** $\tau$. Test $H_0:\rho=0$; correlation ≠ causation.

**Regression** as inference: linear regression coefficients have standard errors and t-tests; logistic regression reports odds ratios $e^{\beta}$; check residual plots, multicollinearity (VIF), heteroscedasticity.

**Bayesian statistics.** $p(\theta|D)\propto p(D|\theta)p(\theta)$. Conjugate example: Beta($a,b$) prior + $k$ successes in $n$ ⇒ Beta($a+k,b+n-k$). Report **credible intervals** (95% probability the parameter lies in the interval *given* data and prior), posterior predictive, Bayes factors. Advantages: uncertainty, priors, small data; costs: prior choice, computation (MCMC, variational).

**Bootstrap.** Resample the data with replacement $B$ times, recompute the statistic, use the percentiles for a CI or the spread for a standard error - works for medians, AUC, differences in F1, anything. **Permutation tests** shuffle labels to build the null (use the lab above).

**Power analysis.** Given effect size $d$, $\alpha$, desired power (0.8): per-group $n\approx2\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}+z_{1-\beta}}{d}\right)^2$ (two-sample, $d=\Delta/\sigma$). Do it *before* running experiments.
tradeoffs: Parametric tests are more powerful when assumptions hold; non-parametric/permutation tests are safer when they don't.
Frequentist p-values are standard in journals; Bayesian reporting is more informative but less conventional.
pitfalls: p-hacking and multiple comparisons without correction.
Using unpaired tests for paired data.
Applying t-tests to heavy-tailed or tiny samples without checking assumptions.
interview: Explain a p-value to a non-statistician.
What is statistical power and how do you compute sample size?
use: Validating model comparisons and any claim in a paper; planning sample sizes.
avoid: Do not report p-values without effect sizes and confidence intervals.

qa.q: Why not run many t-tests instead of ANOVA?
qa.a: Each test has a 5% false-positive chance; for k groups there are k(k−1)/2 comparisons, so the family-wise error rate inflates (≈ 1−0.95^m). ANOVA tests all means at once; follow up with corrected post-hoc tests.

title: Optimisation theory: convexity, Newton, quasi-Newton, L-BFGS, Lagrange multipliers, constrained optimisation
tagline: The classical optimisation toolbox behind SVMs, regression, and every training algorithm.
explain:
**Problem.** $\min_xf(x)$ s.t. $g_i(x)\le0$, $h_j(x)=0$. **Convex set**: segment between any two points stays inside. **Convex function**: $f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)$ ⇔ Hessian PSD. For convex problems every local minimum is global and gradient descent converges ($O(1/t)$, linearly if strongly convex). Convex in ML: linear/ridge/lasso regression, logistic regression, SVM; non-convex: neural nets, k-means, matrix factorisation, mixtures.

**First-order methods.** **Gradient descent** $x\leftarrow x-\eta\nabla f$; **SGD** with minibatches; **mini-batch** trades noise vs speed; **momentum** $v\leftarrow\beta v+\nabla f$; **Nesterov** evaluates the gradient at the look-ahead point $x-\eta\beta v$ (optimal $O(1/t^2)$ for smooth convex). **Adaptive**: AdaGrad (per-parameter accumulation, good for sparse features), RMSProp, Adam/AdamW (see the optimizer lab).

**Newton's method.** Minimise the second-order Taylor model: $x\leftarrow x-H^{-1}\nabla f$. Quadratic convergence near a minimum but costs $O(n^3)$ and needs $H\succ0$ (use damping/line search/trust region). On a quadratic it converges in one step regardless of conditioning.

**Quasi-Newton (BFGS) and L-BFGS.** Approximate $H^{-1}$ from successive gradient differences $s_k=x_{k+1}-x_k$, $y_k=\nabla f_{k+1}-\nabla f_k$ with the secant condition $B_{k+1}s_k=y_k$. BFGS stores a dense matrix ($O(n^2)$); **L-BFGS** stores the last $m$ (5-20) pairs and computes the direction by a two-loop recursion in $O(mn)$ - the default for logistic regression, CRFs, style transfer and small-to-medium smooth problems (scikit-learn, SciPy). Needs a good **line search** (Wolfe conditions). Also **conjugate gradient** for large linear systems.

**Constrained optimisation.** **Lagrangian** $\mathcal L(x,\lambda,\nu)=f(x)+\sum\lambda_ig_i(x)+\sum\nu_jh_j(x)$. **KKT conditions** (necessary, and sufficient for convex): stationarity $\nabla_x\mathcal L=0$, primal feasibility, dual feasibility $\lambda_i\ge0$, **complementary slackness** $\lambda_ig_i(x)=0$. Equality-constrained example: maximise entropy subject to $\sum p=1$ gives the uniform distribution. **Duality**: the dual $\max_{\lambda\ge0}\min_x\mathcal L$ lower-bounds the primal (weak duality); equal for convex problems under Slater's condition. The **SVM** is solved through its dual, which exposes support vectors (non-zero $\lambda_i$) and the kernel trick.

**Other solvers**: projected gradient, penalty/barrier and interior-point methods, ADMM, coordinate descent (lasso), proximal gradient (L1), simplex (linear programming), trust-region methods.

**Regularisation as optimisation**: L2/L1 penalties are Lagrangian forms of norm constraints ($\|w\|\le c$); weight decay; early stopping; **learning-rate scheduling** (step, cosine, warm-up, cyclical).

**Choosing**: small smooth problem → L-BFGS; huge data/deep nets → AdamW/SGD+momentum; sparse features → AdaGrad; L1 penalty → coordinate descent/proximal methods; constraints → KKT/QP solvers.
tradeoffs: Second-order accuracy vs per-step cost; L-BFGS is the practical compromise.
Full-batch methods are deterministic; stochastic ones are noisy but scale and generalise well.
pitfalls: Newton without ensuring $H$ is PD (steps may go uphill).
L-BFGS on noisy stochastic gradients (breaks the secant assumption).
Ignoring feature scaling, which dominates convergence speed.
interview: Why is Newton's method rarely used for deep nets?
Explain KKT complementary slackness in an SVM.
How does L-BFGS avoid storing the Hessian?
use: Choosing the right solver; deriving SVM/regularised objectives; justifying optimisation choices in a paper.
avoid: Do not use batch second-order methods on million-parameter stochastic problems.

qa.q: Why does Newton solve a quadratic in one step?
qa.a: For $f=\tfrac12x^\top Ax-b^\top x$, $\nabla f=Ax-b$ and $H=A$, so $x-H^{-1}\nabla f=x-A^{-1}(Ax-b)=A^{-1}b$, the exact minimiser.
